name: Dermalogen / Autologen

lead: Autologen and Dermalogen are injectable dermal fillers made from human collagen, used to add volume to the lips and soften lines. Autologen is processed from the patient's own skin; Dermalogen is made from donor tissue. The filling is visible after injection.

A 2000 article on facial soft-tissue augmentation described them as physiologic and consistent with many qualities of an ideal dermal filler. A 2004 review classed them as autograft and homograft fillers respectively. Wikipedia says Autologen is absorbed quickly, so results are very temporary, and that some studies suggest Dermalogen lasts somewhat longer than standard collagen.

paras: Human collagen is processed and injected into the skin by a clinician, where it adds volume until the body gradually absorbs it. Results are described as short-to-moderate in duration, so use is repeated if people want to keep the look.
The sources reviewed describe low immune risk because the material is human-derived, with no allergy risk reported for Autologen, and results are temporary. No detailed safety trials were found.

angle.text: Injectable collagen made from the patient's own skin (Autologen) or donor tissue (Dermalogen) adds volume to the lips and softens lines. The filling is visible after injection and is gradually absorbed. Sources describe short-to-moderate persistence and low allergy risk.

lead: Autologen and Dermalogen are injectable dermal fillers made of human tissue collagen matrix. Autologen is processed from the patient's own skin, harvested under local anaesthesia, and Dermalogen is made from donor (allogeneic) tissue.[1][2][3] Injected into lines, folds and areas of lost volume, they are used to smooth wrinkles and restore facial contour, which is how they improve appearance.[1]

A 2000 article in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described dermal augmentation with these matrices as physiologic, appearing ultimately safe and effective, and having many qualities of an ideal filler.[1] A 2001 review reported that results with Dermalogen were comparable with other injectable dermal agents and had the most natural effects, while noting that its absolute longevity had not been fully established.[4] A 2004 review placed Autologen among autografts and Dermalogen among homografts, noting that no perfect filler exists.[2]

Because Autologen comes from the patient, its benefits are described as elimination of local tissue reaction and rejection, though an overview noted it had not been shown to last longer than competitors.[5] Wikipedia's lip augmentation article says Autologen carries no allergy risk but is absorbed rapidly, and that Dermalogen may last slightly longer than standard collagen.[6]
infobox: Described as temporary; Dermalogen possibly longer than bovine collagen[6]

paras: These products belong to the family of collagen fillers that replaced or followed bovine collagen, which required allergy testing.[6] The human-derived versions avoid that requirement in Wikipedia's account.[6] A 2002 review lists them among biologic fillers beside collagen, Isolagen, autologous fat, Fibrel and hyaluronic acid derivatives, and against alloplastic fillers such as silicone and Artecoll.[7] Dermaplant, another allogeneic matrix, was described as commercially available in 2001.[4]

Facial soft-tissue augmentation is used where age-related changes cause contour defects or where patients want volume enhancement; the products are intended for facial lines, scars and volume depletion.[1][7] The 2000 review noted that filler failures stem from poor biocompatibility, technique, or mismatch to the underlying defect.[1]

Autologen has also been used for vocal fold augmentation. A 1995 preliminary study of eight patients used skin harvested under local anaesthesia, processed into an injectable form, to treat vocal fold problems including atrophy and scarring.[3] Dermalogen was compared with other dermal substitutes in a nude-mouse wound model, where each substitute reduced wound contracture.[8]

Authors writing in the early 2000s described the natural results and good biocompatibility of the matrix.[1][4] Longevity depends on facial region, technique and volume injected, and its absolute persistence had not been fully established; the reviewers noted that biomaterials of this kind generally need repeat dosing to maintain effect.[4] An overview of Autologen concluded it had not been proven to outlast competing fillers.[5]

No controlled trials in cosmetic use were found. The literature consists of narrative reviews and clinician accounts: a 2000 review of Autologen and Dermalogen,[1] a 2001 review of Dermalogen and Dermaplant,[4] a 2002 review of collagen and injectable fillers,[7] and a 2004 comparison of injectable categories.[2] Small studies outside cosmetics include the 1995 vocal fold study of eight patients[3] and the mouse wound study.[8]
